desc:
A shop sells items in product families. Each element of items is a triple [group, weight, value]: the item belongs to family group, weighs weight and is worth value. Items of the same family are alternatives of each other, so you may pick at most one item from each family (and none from a family is fine). Items of one family can appear anywhere in the array, not necessarily next to each other.

The total weight of the chosen items must not exceed capacity. Return the maximum total value.

items = [[0,2,3], [0,3,4], [1,4,6], [1,2,2]], capacity = 5 -> 6   (item [1,4,6] alone)
items = [[0,2,3], [0,3,4], [1,4,6], [1,2,2]], capacity = 6 -> 9   ([0,2,3] and [1,4,6])
items = [[7,1,5], [7,1,9]],                   capacity = 5 -> 9   (only one of the two may be used)
constraints: items[i] = [group, weight, value] with 0 ≤ group ≤ 100, 1 ≤ weight ≤ 100, 0 ≤ value ≤ 100,000
hints: The usual item-by-item loop would allow two items of the same family. What should be the unit of the outer loop instead?
Process one family at a time. Let dp[c] be the best value using the families handled so far with total weight at most c.
For a family, build a new table from the old one: new[c] = max(old[c], old[c - w] + v) over every item (w, v) of the family. Always read from old, so two items of the same family are never combined.
editorial: Group the triples by their family id. The knapsack state after finishing some families is the usual array dp[c] (best value with weight at most c). For the next family we have three kinds of choices: take nothing from it, or take exactly one of its items. Hence new[c] = max(dp[c], max over items (w, v) of dp[c - w] + v), and every candidate reads the table from before the family, which makes it impossible to combine two items of the same family.

Computing the new table into a separate array (or iterating capacity downward and looping over the family's items in the innermost loop) both work. Each item is looked at once for each capacity, giving O(n · capacity) time and O(capacity) space. This "group knapsack" pattern shows up whenever choices are mutually exclusive, for example choosing one size per product.
